The eleven ratings for Asker Healthcare

Asker Healthcare (ASKER-SE): the market has priced the bear's reading of Asker's accounts, our base case is better, and the FY2026 annual report will decide between them

Written 24 October 2026. Money in SEK unless stated. Share price SEK 70.8 (21 October); the model uses SEK 71.70 (22 October). Last reported period: Q2 2026. Q3 2026 results: 4 November 2026. The definitions of adjusted EBITA and of the EPS basis used throughout are in the end notes.

#0Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The conclusion in one paragraph. Asker is a good, defensive distribution business run by a strong operator. Management has presented Asker's accounts at their most favourable on every line, and the market now prices the shares as if the least favourable reading of those accounts were true. Over 18 months Asker's operating outcomes are more predictable than the share price's treatment of them: our range for 2027 is revenue within ±2% and adjusted EBITA within -6% to +5% of our base. The equity outcome, by contrast, is binary on one document, the FY2026 annual report, and the skew of that document is modestly positive because the market narrative already assumes the worst of it. Asker is therefore a dated case for the clearing of a cause for concern, in a non-cyclical business on a first-quartile multiple, with the clearing four to six months away. Asker is not a momentum case and not yet a turning one. Nor is it a beat-and-raise compounder (the company has never raised a target), a cash machine (not yet) or a sector call (89% of the daily variance in Asker's share price is specific to Asker).

What Asker is. Asker is Europe's largest brand-neutral distributor of medical supplies, devices and equipment; it does not distribute pharmaceuticals. In 2025 Asker had SEK 16.8bn of sales and adjusted EBITA of SEK 1,594m (a 9.5% margin) from more than 50 companies in 19 countries. Asker runs its subsidiaries in a decentralised way and grows through two engines: 4 to 5% organic growth and 10 to 20 bolt-on acquisitions a year at 6 to 8x EBITA.

Why the shares are back at the listing price. One broker's earnings-quality reconstruction has set the share price. Asker listed in March 2025 at SEK 70; between August and October 2026 DNB Carnegie moved its rating from Buy (target SEK 105) to Sell (SEK 60) to Hold (SEK 66.5) in eight weeks. DNB Carnegie's reconstruction removes capitalised development from adjusted earnings and highlights run-down provisions, software lives stretched to ten years, integration costs treated as non-recurring, and SEK 645m to 1,050m of earn-outs held outside reported net debt. On that reconstruction Asker's 2025 cash EBITA was SEK 1.2bn, 25% below the reported SEK 1.6bn, and Asker's all-in leverage of 3.1 to 3.4x looked close to binding against a 3.50x bank covenant. Three features of the share register amplified the narrative: Interogo owns 40%, the free float is about half the shares, and only USD 6 to 8m of stock trades a day. The CFO's sale of SEK 17.5m of shares in May 2026 added to the doubt.

The seven things that matter, in order of importance

1
The market has priced DNB Carnegie's reconstruction, and our base case is materially better than that reconstruction. Our own forensic review puts Asker's cash EBITA 10 to 15% below adjusted EBITA, not 25% below (the table below sets out each item). The enterprise value of about 15x 2027 adjusted EBITA equals DNB Carnegie's own multiple for cash EBITA applied to the reported figure, so the full discount for the accounting dispute is already in the share price.
2
The market's dominant fear, a forced halt to acquisitions, is misplaced for 2027. About two-thirds to 70% of the model's 2027 adjusted EBITA growth of SEK 238m (12.5%) is secured without a single new acquisition: the organic engine supplies SEK 115 to 130m and the annualisation of the seven 2026 acquisitions about SEK 45m. If Asker stopped acquiring today, 2027 adjusted EBITA would still grow 8 to 9%. The bank covenant also leaves room. The 3.50x covenant uses a definition that excludes leases and long-term earn-outs and includes acquired EBITDA pro forma, and it sits more than a turn above the company's own alternative leverage ratio of 2.43x. Any slowdown in acquisitions would therefore be Asker's choice, not its lenders' decision. No broker covering the stock has written either point.
3
One variable swings the case: Asker's statutory cash conversion. Cash conversion governs leverage headroom (reported leverage is 2.37x against a self-imposed ceiling of 2.5x); leverage headroom governs the acquisition budget; and the acquisition budget governs more than half of Asker's EBITA growth from 2028. Operating cash flow has fallen from about 101% of adjusted EBITA in 2022 to 2024 to a statutory 20% in Q2 2026 (chart below). Inventory days have risen for four years, from 59 to 82, and the model needs them back at 76 by the end of 2027 and 72 by the end of 2028. Asker has not yet shown that recovery at its enlarged scale, so cash conversion is where the real risk in the case sits, for 2028 to 2030 rather than for 2027.
4
Demand is not the question, and it will not become the question. Healthcare volumes did not fall at McKesson or Cardinal in 2008 to 2010. Asker's organic run-rate of 4 to 5% is 1 to 2 points above a market growing 3 to 4%, and one point of organic growth is worth only about 1.2% of EPS. Margin matters five times as much as volume: 50 basis points of adjusted EBITA margin is worth 6% of EPS. The multiple matters more than both: one turn of two-year-forward P/E is SEK 4.63 a share, 6.5% of the share price.
5
The next four months cannot prove the case; the FY2026 annual report (February to April 2027) can. The Q3 2026 report (4 November) will show about 19% adjusted EBITA growth and a weak statutory cash print. The Q4 2026 cash print (February 2027) will look poor against AddLife's print a week earlier for a structural reason rather than a deterioration: Asker has no seasonal fourth-quarter release of working capital of the kind AddLife has. Only the annual report can show Asker's provisions, capitalisation policy, software lives and, perhaps, a leverage definition that includes earn-outs. About 60% of our probability distribution for the annual report is an outcome the share price would receive well.
6
Consensus estimates will fall before they rise, and the narrative and the multiple will turn before the estimates do. On a like-for-like basis, consensus 2027 EPS growth is about four points too high (because of interest and depreciation), consensus 2027 free cash flow is 15 to 25% too high (because of capitalised development) and consensus 2026 EBITDA is 2 to 3% too high (because of double running at the new Gothenburg distribution centre and year-end prudence). Consensus 2028 EBITDA, by contrast, is 6% too low. Over the last twelve months consensus FY2027 EBITDA rose 11% while consensus FY2027 EPS fell 3%, consensus FY2028 EPS fell 14% and the share of Buy ratings fell 17 points; we expect that pattern to continue for two more quarters. The upgrade that matters is a rating, not a number: with three brokers (one Buy at SEK 106 and two Holds at SEK 66.5 and SEK 82), one broker changing its rating after one clean document shifts a third of the rating mix.
7
Most of the return comes from re-rating, which is the return profile a bottoming stock on a first-quartile multiple should offer. At our fair multiple of 20x, in the lower half of the stock's range where Viewforth's guideline puts a bottoming stock, the return to December 2027 is about +31% (26% annualised) and the three-year return is about +42% (14% annualised). Of those returns, earnings supply +21% and +30%, the multiple +7% in each case, and dividends +2% and +4%. At 17x, the multiple we expect if the accounts mildly disappoint and the acquisition engine slows, the 18-month return is +12%. The model's own +52.7% to December 2027 applies about 24x, the median of a nineteen-month listed history set mostly at the pre-dispute premium, to 2029 EPS of SEK 4.63; roughly two-thirds of the model's return is re-rating. The fair trough is SEK 45 to 50 (-30 to -37%), and the shares reach it only through the 5% severe accounting case or a second quarter of near-zero statutory cash flow.

Where we differ from the market. We are more positive than the market on the balance sheet and on earnings quality, and more negative on near-term EPS and cash. The market also treats the 10 to 12% structural margin ceiling of a brand-neutral distributor as a failing specific to Asker; the ceiling is a fact of the business model, which Asker shares with AddLife and its 11.7% cash margin.

The five judgements that move the shares most over one to two years, with the arithmetic

The fair multiple is worth more than all the earnings judgements combined, and cash conversion is the earnings judgement that matters most.

The base case for reference: 2027 adjusted EBITA SEK 2,134m and EPS SEK 3.53; 2028 adjusted EBITA SEK 2,431m and EPS SEK 4.10; 2029 EPS SEK 4.63 (the earnings that the 18-month value capitalises); net financial items SEK 350 to 355m a year; tax 24%; 385m shares.

17x to 24x = SEK 79 to 111 a shareThe range of plausible multiples is worth more than every earnings judgement combined: a SEK 32 spread, 45% of today's share price.

1. The fair multiple (the largest judgement). Each 1.0x of two-year-forward P/E on 2029 EPS of SEK 4.63 is worth SEK 4.63 a share, 6.5% of SEK 71.70. The plausible range of multiples for December 2027 runs from 17x, if Asker's proof cycle stalls, to 24x, if the proof cycle completes in full. No earnings judgement comes close to that SEK 32 spread. Asker's multiple is driven by the company rather than the sector (the R-squared of Asker's returns against the sector basket is 11%), so Asker's own disclosures will move it, not sector rotation.

2. Cash conversion, and through it the acquisition budget (the largest earnings judgement, from 2028). Each SEK 100m spent on acquisitions at 7x EBITA buys SEK 14m of EBITA; after about SEK 5m of interest and 24% tax, that SEK 100m adds SEK 0.018 to EPS. The model funds SEK 0.95bn of new acquisitions in 2027 from free cash flow of about 55% of adjusted EBITA. A conversion rate of 45% or 70% instead moves 2028 EPS by about 6% either way (figure below). For 2027 the range is half as wide, because most of the acquired contribution to 2027 is already in hand.

The indicators that will show which state Asker is in, in the order they arrive:

  1. Inventory days at the Q4 2026 report: below 80 is a pass.
  2. FY2026 statutory operating cash flow above SEK 1.3bn before earn-outs.
  3. Acquisitions announced at SEK 200 to 250m a quarter during 2027.
  4. Reported leverage at or below 2.2x at the end of 2027.

3. The size of the accounting clean-up. The model carries SEK 15m of year-end prudence in Q4 2026 and SEK 25m a year of higher provisioning from 2027, which together cost about 1.2 points of 2027 adjusted EBITA growth. If the FY2026 report instead takes a disclosed one-off charge of SEK 120m into 2027 adjusted EBITA, 2027 EBITA falls to SEK 2,014m (-5.6%) and 2027 EPS to SEK 3.29 ((2,014 - 350) x 0.76 / 384.9m shares), 7% below the base. Reported growth would then print at about 6% against the company's 15% framework, yet the multiple would most likely rise, because the narrative assumes an overstatement of 20 to 25%. In the 5% severe case (an auditor-driven restatement that removes 20% of adjusted EBITA), 2027 EBITA is about SEK 1,700m, 2027 EPS about SEK 2.68, and at 15x the shares are worth about SEK 40.

4. The adjusted EBITA margin (the operating range). Fifty basis points of margin on 2027 revenue of SEK 21.3bn is SEK 107m of EBITA and SEK 0.21 of EPS (6%); carried to 2029, the same 50 basis points is SEK 0.25 of EPS and, at 20x, SEK 5 a share (7%). Our plausible range for the 2027 margin is 9.5% to 10.5% around 10.0%, with a slight negative skew from the risks below.

5. Interest and the other costs below EBITA (the quiet judgement). Consensus has not yet carried about SEK 70 to 100m of pre-tax costs below EBITA, worth SEK 0.14 to 0.20 of EPS (4 to 6%), and those costs are why consensus 2027 EPS growth of 18% will be cut toward 14%. Consensus holds depreciation and amortisation flat at SEK 500m, whereas Gothenburg (SEK 10 to 18m a year from 2027), rising lease depreciation and the amortisation of capitalised development point to SEK 535m in 2027 and SEK 585m in 2028. Consensus also implies net financial items flat at SEK 300 to 316m, against the model's SEK 350 to 355m. On rates, a one-point move is SEK 35m of net financial items and SEK 0.07 of EPS (2%); the Riksbank hike expected in November costs SEK 6m.

Organic growth is deliberately left off this list: one point of organic growth is SEK 20 to 25m of EBITA and SEK 0.04 to 0.05 of EPS (1.2%).

#1Tailwinds in the operating environment; absence of headwinds

Asker's demand environment is stable, visible and slowly growing; if Asker disappoints over the next 18 months, the cause will be internal, not external.

Evidence: the market. The European medtech market was worth about SEK 1,355bn in 2024 and grows 3 to 4% a year. The share of that market handled by value-added distributors rose from 35% in 2019 to 40% in 2023, against about 60% in the United States, and that share gain is the one external force that has accelerated over the last five years. The forces on each side are set out below.

Evidence: Asker's organic growth. Asker's organic growth printed 6, 3, 5, -1, 5 and 5% over the last six quarters. SEK 350m of Nordic defence and preparedness orders in 2024 explain the two weak quarters entirely, and those orders have now washed out of the comparison; once they did, Asker's North business area grew 10% organically in Q2 2026.

Inference. The tailwinds add 1 to 2 points of growth above the market, and no more; nothing at the level of demand has changed in six months. The headwinds differ in speed: price pressure is structural and slow, OEM reclamation of a device line is specific to that line and sudden when it comes, and the financial environment is strong now. Management's push toward advanced devices (about 70% of medtech activity) creates an asymmetry: the device mix raises Asker's gross margin and, at the same time, raises the share of revenue exposed to an OEM bypassing the distributor.

So what. Build Asker's revenue with confidence: 4 to 5% organic growth, no price increases above inflation, and a currency effect of -1.5% in 2027. Expect no external excuse for a demand shortfall over 18 months. The external world does not justify assuming cheaper debt or a higher multiple; Asker must earn a higher multiple through disclosure.

Strongest counter-case. A squeeze on European public finances (French government bonds at 152 basis points over German in October 2026) could reach Asker through tender pricing rather than volume, and the German cap lands inside our horizon; distributors typically absorb a third to a half of reimbursement cuts. If that pressure coincided with an OEM going direct in a large category, Asker's organic growth would drift to 3% and, in DNB Carnegie's own words, the compounder label would be lost regardless of acquisitions.

What would change our view. Organic growth below 3% for two consecutive quarters that comparisons do not explain; a disclosed OEM contract loss in a line above SEK 30m of sales; a re-tender by a Dutch insurer.

Versus the market. Consensus and the narrative treat demand as fine, and we agree. We differ in one respect: the narrative gives Asker no credit for the structural gain in distributors' market share.

Score: 52. A defensive, visible, slowly growing market with a small structural share gain, offset by price-led procurement, OEM bypass and a hostile financing regime: average for a European listed company, and better than average on predictability.

#2Internally-driven corporate change forces; absence of problems

Asker's positive internal changes are real but modest and cash-constrained; the change that would move the multiple, conservative reporting, has not yet been made, and the FY2026 report is the test of it.

Evidence: people and governance. Asker's executive core has been unchanged for a decade or more: CEO Johan Falk since 2012, the CFO since 2019 and the COO since 2013. The board was refreshed at the top in May 2026, when Mikael Stöhr (formerly of Coor and Consolis) became Chair; Mr Stöhr holds 291,970 call options at SEK 94.90, issued by Interogo and bought at fair value. Interogo's investment director joined the board and its Audit Committee in December 2025.

Evidence: a shift in emphasis from land-grab to digestion. Asker's strategy is unchanged, but within twelve months the CEO's language has moved from "never seen such a good pipeline" (July 2025) to "gradual realisation of benefits" and "focus on cash flow and capital efficiency" (July 2026). Asker abandoned the Kirstine Hardam acquisition (about SEK 200m of sales) after a year-long Danish competition review.

Inference. The positive internal forces could add perhaps 50 to 80 basis points of margin in combination by 2028, and all of them draw on the same scarce resource: cash. The negative forces are present now, and they are the reason the stock is back at its listing price. The one internal change that would move the multiple is one that management has not yet made: adopting the conservative reporting standards of the listed cohort of Nordic acquirers. The new Chair, the owner's representative on the Audit Committee, the public challenge and the de-rating together give management both the motive and the opportunity to make that change, and the July 2026 language says the direction has been chosen.

So what. Take the operating lines that management steers (organic growth, the pace of acquisitions, business-area margins) at roughly their stated levels, and discount the lines it does not steer (free cash flow, leverage after earn-outs, EPS) by 10 to 20% against the company's presentation. Expect a voluntary tightening of accounting in early 2027 that lowers adjusted EBITA growth by a few points and raises the multiple by more. Asker's internal story is AddLife's story of 2023 to 2025 (deleverage, prove cash, re-rate), started from better organic growth and a worse accounting reputation.

Strongest counter-case. Insider ownership does not guarantee conservative reporting. The CEO holds 9.06m shares, but the LTIP pays 85% on adjusted EBITA growth, so the incentive still rewards capitalising costs and adding them back. The board has twice declined internal audit, and the CFO who built the leverage definition also runs investor relations. If the FY2026 report changes nothing, the discount persists and the "false friend" path opens: adjusted EBITA grows 15% while cash, leverage and the pace of acquisitions deteriorate.

What would change our view. Up: a leverage ratio re-presented to include contingent consideration; a cash-conversion target; an internal audit function; a capital markets day. Down: a second quarter of statutory operating cash flow near zero outside earn-out effects; further unexplained senior departures (two second-tier heads left in 2026); a repriced acquisition or a second blocked one.

Versus the market. The narrative treats management as "tolerating aggressive accounting" and the Chair as decorative. We see a motivated Chair with real capital at risk and a management team that has already changed its language, and we put 60% on a disclosure outcome that the market receives well. The market has not priced the possibility that the accounting clean-up is the catalyst rather than the risk.

Score: 48. Genuine but modest, dated and cash-constrained positive change, set against present negatives in reporting, working capital and leverage: slightly below average, with the balance resting on one document.

#3Value chain, industry structure, business model, financial profile and management

Asker is a sound, capital-light distributor with bounded moats and a structural margin ceiling; the market pays the listed cohort for cash conversion, organic growth and clean accounts, and Asker has only the second today.

Industry structure and value chain. The industry is unconcentrated and consolidating slowly. It has 37,000 companies; the top ten value-added distributors held about 21% of the market in 2023, up from 15% in 2019. On the supply side, Asker's top 25 suppliers, out of more than 2,000, account for about 48% of its cost of goods, and none accounts for more than 7%. Market shares are stable at national level: Asker is number one or two in Sweden, Norway and Finland, where system sales make up 79% of Swedish and Norwegian revenue, and Asker re-won 88% of its contracts and won 69% of all tenders it entered in 2024; outside those three countries Asker's share is below 10% everywhere.

Competitors are rational and put margin first, so there is no price war to model; the pricing pressure comes from buyers and is structural. AddLife targets a 45% return on working capital and bought Unicam and Lehnen at under 7x; Uniphar enforces a 12 to 15% return hurdle; and the four Nordic serial acquirers paid a median 6.8x EV/EBITA in 2023 to 2025. The profit pool is thin by design: brand-neutral distributors earn EBITA margins of 9 to 12%, against 18 to 23% at product owners such as Lagercrantz and Lifco, and that gap is "not fixable by execution".

Business model and moats. Asker has four moats of moderate strength:

  1. System-sales lock-in. Asker bundles tens of thousands of items with logistics, training and IT integration, which turns Asker into the customer's supply department and is why re-wins run at 88%.
  2. Regulatory and compliance scale under MDR and IVDR.
  3. Logistics density: Gothenburg, the Dutch warehouse, and 570,000 direct-to-patient patients in the Netherlands (up from 80,000 in 2015). OEMs cannot replicate the direct-to-patient channel because they lack the infrastructure for frequent small home deliveries.
  4. A private-label layer of 10 to 15% of sales, which carries a higher gross margin and gives Asker bargaining power with OEMs.

These moats are distribution-grade. They protect market share and customer relationships, but they do not confer pricing power above inflation or a margin above 10 to 12%, and in the growing device mix they are exposed to OEMs taking distribution back. The addressable market is not the constraint on growth (Asker has about 3% of a SEK 556bn distributor segment, 800 priority targets and 11,000 to 33,000 candidates); capital is the constraint.

Financial profile. Asker is above average on the measures that count for a distributor and below average on the measures the market is now looking at.

Reported net income was only 31% of adjusted EBITA in 2025 because three items sit between the two: SEK 341m of amortisation of acquired intangibles, SEK 204m of items affecting comparability and SEK 350m of net financial items. Cash tax paid (SEK 337m in 2025, 21% of adjusted EBITA) runs well above the reported tax charge (SEK 149m) for two reasons: amortisation on share deals is not tax-deductible anywhere in Europe, and the deferred tax liability (SEK 585m) unwinds through the income statement as a non-cash credit.

Management. Asker's CEO is a strong operator with a rare profile: McKinsey, Getinge, 14 years at OneMed and Asker, and about SEK 640m of personal stock. He built a pan-European platform from a Nordic distributor, compounded adjusted EBITA at 38% a year from 2019 to 2024 and by 17% in 2025, bought more than 60 companies at disciplined prices (a three-year incremental return of about 23%), walked away from one, and has delivered every stated target since listing. The wider team is stable and adequate rather than outstanding. Asker's culture delivers organic growth and working-capital discipline (an engagement score of 76 against a target of 70) but is under strain (staff turnover of 17.3% against AddLife's 10%; sick leave above target). Asker's ambition is the largest in the listed cohort: EBITA growth above 15% with no end date, 10 to 20 acquisitions a year, and France, Spain and Italy as markets still to enter.

Management's gap is its standards below the EBITA line. Asker has no cash-first culture of the Lagercrantz kind; it discloses neither acquisition economics nor subsidiary margins, covenants or a price-volume bridge; its consensus is compiled by the company from unnamed contributors; and it publishes an "adjusted cash flow from operating activities" that adds back earn-outs paid.

Inference and so what. Asker's structure supports 4 to 5% organic growth, a gross margin that rises only through mix, a decade-long acquisition runway, and a reported adjusted EBITA margin of 10.4 to 10.7% by 2028 to 2030. The structure does not support AddLife's 12% margin without a rise in the share of proprietary products, which Asker does not plan. The cohort's precedents are unusually clear about what the market pays for: cash conversion that funds acquisitions without leverage rising, organic growth above 3 to 4%, and clean accounts.

Strongest counter-case. Scale has not yet produced operating leverage. Revenue per employee is down 20%, and purchasing synergies have been "elusive" in Germany, where acquired companies already bought more cheaply than the group. The decentralised model (85% local freedom, 45 central staff, no internal audit) sees local problems late. And 51% of sales now sit in the West business area at a 9.6% margin and 18% in Central at 9.2%, against North's 13.6%, so every point of sales mix that shifts away from North costs about 4 basis points of group margin.

What would change our view. Up: disclosure of the economics of acquired companies at subsidiary level, and a stated capital-allocation hierarchy (deleverage to a stated level, then acquire, then return cash). Down: evidence that founders leave after the three-year earn-outs of the 2022 to 2023 acquisitions expire in 2026 to 2027; peers' experience says one departing founder is replaced by two or three hires, which dilutes the subsidiary's margin.

Versus the market. The narrative compares Asker unfavourably with AddLife on margin and leverage. On DNB Carnegie's own like-for-like figures, the two companies have nearly identical lease-inclusive leverage (2.8 to 2.9x) and similar returns on working capital. AddLife deserves a small premium for accounting quality and three years of proven deleveraging, but not the 10-point gap in trailing P/E (29.4x against 19.7x) that the market has opened.

Score: 55. A sound, defensive, capital-light distribution model with real but bounded moats, top-decile working-capital returns and a capable owner-operator, held back by a structural margin ceiling, low reported ROCE and reporting standards below the cohort's best.

#4Conservative guidance, expectation management, track record of delivery and raising

Asker's financial framework is a floor, not a forecast, and management never raises it, so upgrades will come from the sell-side rather than from guidance.

Evidence: the framework. Asker gives no numerical guidance. Its standing framework has not changed since the prospectus and has never been raised, although rolling adjusted EBITA growth has run at 17 to 22% in every period since listing and the rolling margin has reached 9.8%. The one change went the other way: in 2024 Asker tightened its leverage target from a range of 2.0 to 3.0x to a ceiling of 2.5x.

Evidence: the record. Against broker estimates Asker's adjusted EBITA record is good: beats of 4 to 7% in four of the last six quarters, one quarter in line and one 2% short, and 17% growth in 2025 against the 15% floor. Against cash the record is weakening, as #0 shows. Consensus for 2026 (EBITDA +20.9%, EPS +20.8%) sits above the framework because it extrapolates the first half's 23% growth. Consensus for 2027 (EBITDA +10.2%) sits below the framework, because the sell-side has stopped believing that the acquired engine can grow EBITA by 10 to 12% a year without leverage rising. Management's informal commentary runs ahead of its formal framework: "excellent pipeline visibility", "already discussing targets for Q4 2026 and Q1 2027", and "capital under the 2.5x ceiling is the constraint, not deal availability".

Inference. The framework is undemanding against Asker's record, realistic against the next three years, and silent below EBITA. There is no beat-and-raise staircase to ride, because management does not raise its targets: the beats happen quietly, and upgrades, when they come, come from the sell-side. On the model, Asker's rolling growth falls below 15% at the Q2 2027 report in July 2027, which is when the market will register the 2027 miss. The margin target is touched only at the FY2027 report, not at Q4 2026 as the company's own trajectory once suggested. A re-presentation of the framework under the new Chair (earn-outs in leverage, a cash target, a first capital markets day) has a probability of 30 to 40%.

So what. Do not expect a guidance-raise catalyst. Expect a mid-2027 headline of "rolling growth below 15%" that is already in consensus numbers (7% acquired growth) but not yet in the narrative. Expect the one target the company can claim as met, the margin, to arrive at the edge of the window rather than to soften the FY2026 disclosures. The useful signal is management's qualitative pipeline commentary, which supports modelling acquired growth above the brokers' 7% and below the framework's 10 to 12%.

Strongest counter-case. The absence of guidance cuts both ways. Asker has no guidance to cut, so a bad quarter produces a broker revision rather than a profit warning; but coverage is thin (three brokers on FactSet, with DNB Carnegie supplying nearly all the research), so a single broker note moves both the consensus and the share price, as September 2026 showed.

What would change our view. A capital markets day with a cash-flow framework and disclosure of acquisition economics would move this score by ten points; none is announced, and the company has never held one. A formal cut to the growth target (10 to 15% probability) would confirm a chosen slowdown and cost 3 to 5 points of 2028 growth.

Versus the market. The market reads "consensus below the framework" as conservatism waiting to be beaten. We read the sell-side's 7% acquired growth as a judgement about cash, not as sandbagging, and we expect management to present 2027's 12 to 13% growth against the framework's 15% as "in line over time".

Score: 42. A floor-not-forecast framework that is never raised, a good adjusted-EBITA beat record, a weakening cash record and no guidance below EBITA: below average on the beat-and-raise dimension Richard cares about most.

#5Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out scope, feedback loops

Revenue growth does not turn into outsized profit growth at Asker: pricing power is defensive only, operating leverage is modest, and the balance sheet throttles the acquisition engine for the next 12 to 18 months.

Pricing power: defensive and demonstrated, offensive and absent. Asker held its gross margin at about 41% through the inflation of 2022 to 2025, its public contracts are index-linked, and in Q1 2026 the CFO ruled out a squeeze from the supply chain. Asker discloses no price-volume bridge, however, and like-for-like tender prices fall 2 to 3% a year. Price supplied at most 10 of the 110 basis points of gross-margin gain in Q2 2026 (figure below). The model's gross margin on the company's definition is 41.6%, 41.8% and 42.0% for 2026 to 2028, all from mix, with nothing from price.

Operating leverage: moderate and driven by margin. Cost of goods is about 59% of sales, selling costs about 25% and administration about 9%. The fixed layer (45 central staff) is under 2% of sales, and the large semi-fixed layer flexes with volume, because local managers are steered on return on working capital and add service staff as they add device business. In H1 2026, 5% organic sales growth produced 7% organic adjusted EBITA growth: an incremental margin of about 14% against a 9.9% average, a gearing of 1.3 to 1.4x that matches management's own framework of 5 to 8% organic EBITA growth. The device mix that lifts gross margin also needs more installation, service and sales staff, so, in the CFO's words, "the eventual EBITA benefit is smaller than the gross-margin gain"; in Q2 2026 a 110 basis-point gross-margin gain became a 50 basis-point EBITA-margin gain. Downside gearing is small and transient: AddLife's margin fell 110 basis points sequentially in Q3 2026 when Spanish strikes removed volume, and Oriola's lost quarter in Q2 2020 reversed within one quarter.

Financial leverage: high on every measure and at the self-imposed limit, yet more than a turn inside the covenant. Asker's bank covenant of 3.50x uses a definition that excludes leases and long-term earn-outs and includes acquired EBITDA pro forma, so the company's own measures, not DNB Carnegie's all-in reconstruction, are the relevant comparison.

Leverage matters to the case in two ways. First, interest is a large cost: net financial items of SEK 350m consumed 22% of adjusted EBITA in 2025, and the share falls to 17% in 2026, about 16% in 2027 and 12% by 2030 as EBITDA grows against flat-to-drifting net debt, so a 10% shortfall in EBITA is a 12% shortfall in pre-tax profit. Second, leverage is an input to growth: each 0.1x of headroom under 2.5x is about SEK 200m of acquisition capacity, SEK 28m of EBITA and 1.5 points of EBITA growth. The cohort's rule is that the acquisition engine runs freely below 2.0x, runs under market doubt between 2.0x and 2.5x, and stops above 2.5x: AddLife stopped for two years at 3.5x, Storskogen stopped at 4.35x, and Vimian needed a SEK 1.5bn directed share issue at 4.3x. Asker spends 2026 and 2027 in the middle band.

Cost-out scope: small and concentrated in one programme. The gross benefit is about SEK 80 to 110m a year by 2028 (35 to 45 basis points): Gothenburg SEK 55 to 60m from 2028, product pruning SEK 20 to 30m, and normalisation of integration cost SEK 10 to 20m. Against that benefit sit SEK 30 to 40m of double running in H2 2026 and H1 2027, SEK 10 to 18m of new depreciation and SEK 40m of provisioning normalisation. Asker has no other levers: no purchasing synergy (the decentralised Nordic acquirers deliberately forgo it), no central cost cut (the company needs more control resource, not less) and nothing from warehouse AI before 2029. AddLife's 160 basis points of self-help is not available to Asker, because Asker has no loss-making digital unit to close, no central function to dismantle and no business to divest.

Feedback loops: the balancing loops dominate for 12 to 18 months, and the reinforcing loops are throttled, not broken. The binding loop runs from cash conversion to leverage headroom to the acquisition budget to EBITA growth. The reinforcing loops re-engage from H2 2027 only if free cash flow before acquisitions reaches about 55 to 60% of adjusted EBITA. Acquired mix is a two-edged loop: Asker cherry-picks targets with margins above 10% (acquired companies were consolidated at a 17% margin in H1 2026), which raises gross margin but also raises exposure to OEMs. Inventory days rose because acquired companies temporarily dilute Asker's working-capital efficiency.

Inference and so what. Each engine transmits growth weakly. Organic sales growth of 4.5% becomes organic EBITA growth of 6 to 7%, a gearing of 1.3 to 1.4x. The acquired engine adds 7% to EBITA a year at a cost of SEK 1bn of cash. Financial leverage subtracts about two points from EPS growth relative to EBITA growth until 2028 and adds about two points from 2028. Beyond the per-unit sensitivities in the five judgements above, one more is worth carrying: 1% on the krona is SEK 3.7m of EBITA. The width of outcomes widens down the income statement: the EBITA range is a margin range, the EPS range is a margin-plus-interest range, and the cash range is wider than both, because inventory alone moves SEK 220m for every five days.

Strongest counter-case. If cash conversion recovers to the level of 2022 to 2024 (about 100% for operating cash flow and 70 to 80% for free cash flow), the reinforcing loops re-engage a year early, acquired growth runs at 9 to 10%, leverage reaches 2.0x in 2027, and the model's EBITA for 2028 to 2030 is 5 to 8% too low. Asker had that capability at a smaller scale under private ownership; what is undemonstrated is the same capability at twice the size, with SEK 645m of earn-outs outstanding.

What would change our view. The four cash indicators listed under judgement 2; a disclosed price-volume bridge showing real price increases on renewals of system-sales contracts (no such bridge exists today).

Versus the market. The narrative says "the operating leverage is not there", and it will say so loudest from Q3 2026 to Q2 2027, when year-on-year margin gains narrow to 20 to 30 basis points because of double running at Gothenburg. We expect that window rather than being surprised by it, and we expect Q3 2027 to be the first quarter in which the cost line helps the margin.

Score: 40. No real pricing power, modest and margin-dominated operating leverage, high financial leverage that currently subtracts from EPS growth, one dated cost programme worth 30 basis points, and reinforcing loops that are throttled by the balance sheet for 12 to 18 months.

#6Forecast financials; scope for double-digit growth and for higher growth and margins than the past

The model is a slower, cleaner and more cash-generative version of Asker's last four years, with a trough in the middle: adjusted EBITA compounds at about 13% and EPS at about 16% to 2030.

The inputs behind the forecasts. Each input is set from evidence rather than from the company's framework; the most important are below.

Against consensus. The model's 2027 growth is above consensus, from a lower base. The model is in line with consensus on revenue for 2026 and 2027 and 2.5% above for 2028, where one broker assumes 4% growth. The model's EBITDA is 2.3% below consensus for 2026, 0.6% below for 2027 and 6.3% above for 2028, so its 2027 growth (12.5% for EBITA) is above consensus (10% for EBITDA). The model's EBIT and net income print about 30% above consensus, but that gap is a difference of definition: the model's EBITA excludes the amortisation of acquired intangibles that consensus EBIT includes. The EPS gaps (+11.5%, +7.5% and +8.8%) are also largely definitional; on EPS growth the model is above consensus for 2026, four points below for 2027 and two points above for 2028. Free cash flow for 2027 is 15 to 25% below consensus on a like-for-like basis.

Scope for double-digit growth and for better than the past: yes on both counts, with qualifications. Adjusted EBITA compounds at about 13% over 2025 to 2030 and EPS at about 16%, because the interest share of EBITA falls. Both rates are double digit, but both are below the past's 17 to 38% and below the 15% framework from 2027. The margin rises at the same pace as in 2023 to 2025 (about 30 basis points a year), but from 2028 the gains come from higher-quality sources: the provisioning releases that added about 80 basis points cumulatively over 2023 to 2025 stop and partly reverse, while logistics savings and pruning arrive. Reported net income rises from 31% to 54% of adjusted EBITA; reported ROCE stays at 8 to 9%.

Free cash flow before acquisitions roughly triples from the 2026 trough to 2028, for three reasons, two of them mechanical and dated: the Gothenburg capital spending ends (+SEK 300m against 2025), earn-outs normalise (+SEK 200 to 300m against 2026), and inventory releases cash (+SEK 150 to 200m a year), which depends on behaviour rather than mechanics.

Ranges for 2027: the outcomes widen down the income statement. The lower bound of the EBITA range admits a 10 to 20% probability of a SEK 100 to 150m one-off charge. The EPS range is skewed negatively because interest and depreciation can only disappoint, and the free cash flow range is skewed negatively by inventory and the timing of earn-outs.

Strongest counter-case. The model may be too generous in three ways. First, on the accounting clean-up it sits at the optimistic end of the Financial Analyst's own base-case language: it carries about 1 point of drag on 2027 growth against a described 3 to 6 points. Second, it rests on an inventory reversal the company has not yet shown. Third, the lines for 2029 to 2030 deserve half the weight of 2027's, because the acquired component is a decision made each year, not a trend. A probability-weighted path is the right base for a model with no bear case, but a reader should know that 2027 adjusted EBITA of SEK 2,134m is SEK 40 to 100m above what the most likely clean-up outcome implies.

What would change the forecasts. Up: FY2026 statutory operating cash flow above SEK 1.3bn before earn-outs with inventory days below 78, which would raise the 2027 acquisition budget by SEK 300 to 400m and 2028 EBITA by 3 to 4%; a new preparedness order cycle. Down: a second near-zero statutory cash quarter outside earn-outs, which would cut the acquisition budget to SEK 0.8bn and the leverage headroom to nil; an auditor-driven catch-up (-SEK 100 to 150m on 2027 EBITA); the loss of a device line.

Versus the market. We are in line with consensus on revenue, slightly below on 2026 to 2027 EBITDA, above on 2028, and below on 2027 EPS growth and free cash flow. We read the company's framework as met in 2026 and missed narrowly in 2027; the margin target is met from 2027 on the reported definition but never on a cash definition (8.6 to 8.8% in 2027). We carry the remaining differences of view (the size of the clean-up, the pace of acquisitions) as named scenarios around a probability-weighted base rather than as changed lines.

Score: 58. Double-digit EBITA and mid-teens EPS compounding with rising margins and a tripling of free cash flow from a trough, predictable on revenue and EBITA, less so on cash, and below both the framework and the company's own past.

#7Scope for upgrades to guidance, sell-side estimates and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

Over six months the scope for upgrades lies in the rating mix and the narrative, not in the estimates; over twelve months it lies in both, conditional on the FY2026 annual report.

Evidence: the dated staircase to April 2027. Every step is known to the market, so every step is a proof rather than a discovery. The deciding step is the FY2026 annual report, with the probabilities set out in #0.

Evidence: the estimate changes due. The cuts come first: 2026 EBITDA by 1 to 3%; 2027 EPS by 3 to 5%, as Nordea and the third broker (whose name is restricted) adopt our points on interest and depreciation; and 2027 free cash flow by 15 to 25%, when the annual report publishes capitalised development. The upgrades available in the numbers come later: 2028 EBITDA (+6% on the model) and 2027 EBITDA growth (toward 12% from 10%, as the 2026 base falls).

Inference: the reversal is specific. DNB Carnegie's return to Buy has a 35 to 40% probability within 18 months of a clean annual report, because DNB Carnegie's valuation of 15x EV to cash EBITA moves with any evidence that cash EBITA is above its SEK 1.2bn reconstruction. Nordea's Buy at SEK 106 is the rating most at risk of moving to Hold first (25 to 30% within six months). The upside in the narrative is larger than its novelty, for two reasons: the multiple has further to recover than the earnings have to grow, and three points that no broker has yet written are each a positive surprise waiting for an author. Those three points are that two-thirds of 2027 growth is secured, that the covenant's definition leaves more than a turn of headroom, and that the gap in free cash flow is a difference of definition.

So what: sequence matters. The next two prints (Q3 2026 and Q4 2026) land on lines where consensus is too high, and the market has stopped paying for the line where consensus is right. The following two prints (the annual report, then Q3 2027, when Gothenburg savings first show in North's margin) land on the lines the market prices. A holder before February 2027 is paid for bearing the risk of the document; a holder after it is paid for the proof cycle.

Strongest counter-case. The dominant broker has already moved from Sell to "balanced", so the surprise from clean accounts is smaller than it would have been in September. A mild clean-up would produce a one-day negative reaction before its one-quarter positive. The Q4 cash print will be read against AddLife's seasonal collection a week earlier, even though the comparison is structurally unfair. If the annual report changes nothing (35%), the discount persists for another year and the narrative hardens into "levered roll-up".

What would change our view. A Q3 2026 statutory cash print that is weak for reasons beyond earn-outs and Gothenburg inventory would move the clean-up probabilities toward the severe end. A Q3 print with inventory days flat or down would move them the other way and bring the turn forward.

Versus the market. The market expects the next upgrades to come from EBITA beats. We expect EBITA beats to be ignored, the estimates to be cut first, and the upgrades to come from a disclosure document and then a cash print.

Score: 45. Real but conditional scope, dated to a document four to six months away, with estimate cuts due first and a one-broker narrative that could reverse by a third on one clean report.

#8Current momentum: guidance, sell-side, narrative, technicals, and peers

Momentum is absent or negative on every axis except valuation, and the closest peer, AddLife, sits at the opposite end of every reading.

Technical momentum: F. The share price of SEK 70.8 sits just above its 50-day average (SEK 68.9) and below its 150-day (SEK 74.4) and 200-day (SEK 73.4, -3.5%) averages. The 200-day average has risen in none of the last twelve months, relative strength is at the 20th percentile of the universe, and the 52-week range is SEK 56.2 to 95.1.

Sell-side earnings momentum: C, with a negative component. Consensus FY2027 EPS is unchanged over one and three months, +1% over six months and -3% over twelve months, while consensus FY2027 EBITDA is +11% and sales +5% over twelve months. The mean target price is down 8% over three months, the share of Buy ratings is down 17 points to 67%, and the revision-momentum score is 3.

Guidance and narrative momentum. Asker has no guidance momentum, by construction. The narrative has been negative since 10 September and softened to "balanced" on 1 October, while investor forums remain anchored on the CFO's share sale. No short position above the 0.5% disclosure threshold has been reported, and securities lending has not risen.

Peers. AddLife, the closest peer, is downgraded but strong: DNB Carnegie cut AddLife to Hold on 22 October "after a strong run" despite a Q3 beat (EPS SEK 1.05 against 0.86 expected), and its 12-month return is +5.6%. The wider cohort of serial acquirers (Lifco, Addtech, Indutrade) is in an upgrade cycle driven by currency and cyclical recovery that Asker is not part of. Lagercrantz's fifteen-year streak of EPS growth ended with a 3 to 5% miss in Q1 2026/27, and its multiple fell from 23x. The sector basket is up about 20% over six months while Asker is flat; Asker's daily returns have a correlation of 0.33 with the basket, a beta of 0.90 and an R-squared of 11%.

Inference. Momentum is absent or negative on every axis at Asker and positive at AddLife, which widens the relative gap and will make any turn at Asker more visible when it comes. Asker has not benefited from the flow of "healthcare as the home for tech dollars" (Jefferies' phrase), because the variance of Asker's shares is specific to Asker. The marginal holder since September has been a seller and institutions are waiting for the accounts, but Interogo (40.2%) and SEB (6%) are not sellers.

So what. Asker does not have momentum on its side, and nothing before 4 November will change that. The first technical signal worth acting on would be the 200-day average turning up, which on the current price path cannot happen before early 2027. The contrast with AddLife is both the trap and the opportunity: two companies with the same business model and the same like-for-like leverage, one at the 91st percentile of its P/E range and one at the 9th, separated by three years of proven deleveraging and one forensic note.

Strongest counter-case. Negative momentum in a thin stock, with a 50% free float and USD 6 to 8m of daily trading, can persist long after the fundamentals have turned. A short-seller report remains the most obvious sentiment risk in the cohort: the Montier C-score flags Asker on all six of its criteria, and Lifco fell 16% on a short report in January 2026.

What would change our view. Two consecutive weeks above the 200-day average; a first positive revision to FY2027 EPS from Nordea or the restricted broker; a disclosed institutional buyer.

Versus the market. We agree with the dashboard's readings, with one addition: the C for sell-side momentum flatters Asker. The composite score is lifted by rising EBITDA, which masks the falling EPS and cash components, and EPS and cash are what the stock trades on.

Score: 22. Technical F, revisions C with a negative component, no guidance to move, a one-broker negative narrative, and the closest peer at the opposite end of every reading.

#9Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

The case is simple and its risk is concentrated: predictable at the operating level, binary at the equity level until one document is published.

One swing variable

Statutory cash conversion

Three dated tests

FY2026 cash and inventory (Feb 2027); FY2026 accounts (Feb to Apr 2027); Gothenburg in North's margin (Q3 2027)

Two-thirds secured

2027 EBITA growth, whatever the tests show

Simplicity of the case. Beyond the one variable and three tests above, the demand line contributes almost nothing to the width of outcomes. The drivers of the difference between forecast and history are concentrated for growth: the acquired contribution falling from 12 to 13% of sales to 7% explains about 70% of the revenue deceleration. They are diffuse for margin: five or six items of 10 to 30 basis points each, all dated and internal. They are concentrated in three items for cash: Gothenburg capital spending ending and earn-outs normalising, both mechanical, and inventory days falling, which is behavioural. Four of the six deciding drivers are disclosed quarterly; the two accounting drivers are disclosed annually.

Fragilities and requirements. The forecasts require the two capabilities that have deteriorated most in two years, inventory discipline and cash conversion, to recover while Asker runs its first large automated warehouse and answers a public accounting challenge. They also require one capability Asker has never shown, conservative reporting, to appear without a shock. They do not require any capability the company lacks in kind: no new product, no greenfield market, no pricing power and no central cost programme. The consistency of the forecasts rests on one management choice: to set the acquisition budget from cash and hold the 2.5x ceiling. Spending up to the covenant instead would raise EBITA in 2027 to 2028 and worsen leverage, interest and the multiple.

Share-price risks, ranked by expected impact. The largest risk is an accounting event, voluntary or forced, and the annual report will resolve it one way or the other. The September 2026 fall has reduced the reward to a short-seller but not the material available to one. Risks 5 to 7 would arrive without warning, and no one covering the stock has written about them.

Sector cyclicality and precedents. Healthcare distribution has no demand cycle: McKesson grew gross profit 9% a year through 2008 to 2010, Cardinal's medical segment expanded its margin in fiscal 2010, and Indutrade's 2020 margin was a record. The sector's cycle is a credit and accounting cycle, and its precedents are consistent:

  • Leverage. Levered acquirers that reached 3.5 to 4.4x (AddLife in 2023, Storskogen and Vimian in 2022) paused acquisitions for about two years and missed EBITA expectations by 15 to 30%. Their multiples began to recover eight to nine quarters after the leverage peak, coinciding with the annual report or cash print that confirmed leverage at or below 2.2 to 2.3x, a leadership change, or resumed acquisitions. None fully regained its pre-crisis multiple within 24 months: AddLife traded at 17.6x forward EV/EBITA in April 2026 against 22x before; Vimian at 17x against a 25x average; Storskogen at 10 to 12x, up from 8x.
  • Earnings-quality attacks. These hit share prices fast (Lifco -16%; Asker -20% against AddLife). Where provisions were rebuilt, as in Storskogen's SEK 65m of "tidying", the rebuild produced one-off hits before the recovery.
  • Distribution-centre programmes. These slipped at Uniphar (go-live deferred to February 2027, EUR 20m of extra capital) and Oriola (a year's delay, EUR 54m of extra cost), and never arrived early.

Asker's position in that pattern is better than the precedents'. Asker's leverage peaked at a lower level (2.4x reported) than any of theirs, the critique came from a broker rather than a short-seller, and the de-rating has already taken the stock to a first-quartile multiple. If the precedents hold, Asker's recovery clock started in September 2026, and the first re-rating event sits four to six months out rather than eight quarters.

The trough. A fair trough is SEK 45 to 50, 30 to 37% below the share price. Two routes give that figure: 14 to 15x two-year-forward P/E on 2027 EPS cut by 10%, or 13x EV/EBITA on cash-adjusted 2027 EBITA of about SEK 1,850m with lease-inclusive net debt of SEK 5.7bn. A stress trough is SEK 32 to 38: the severe accounting case at 12x, or acquisitions halted and SEK 2.1 of adjusted EPS at 15x. The 52-week low of SEK 56.2 is where the first wave of sellers stopped, not a floor.

Inference and so what. A simple case with concentrated risk is the right shape for a case Richard can monitor. Asker is predictable at the operating level and unpredictable at the equity level until the annual report is published. The skew is negative at the EPS and cash lines, from dated internal items, and positive at the multiple, because the narrative has priced the worst reading. The distribution around SEK 71 is roughly symmetric in distance and asymmetric in probability: the trough needs one adverse disclosure event (10 to 20%), while the upside needs four to six quarters of proof. The twelve-month probability-weighted centre is about SEK 75 to 85, and the most likely path is a range-bound stock to February 2027 followed by a conditional re-rating.

Strongest counter-case. Simplicity is not safety. A single variable on which the company is currently failing, a binary event with a fat lower tail, a thin register, and a sector precedent in which no company regained its prior multiple within two years add up to a riskier profile than Asker's operating predictability suggests.

Versus the market. The market treats the main risk as a forced halt to acquisitions within 18 months. We treat a forced halt as remote, because covenant headroom is more than a turn, and we see the realistic bad case as a chosen slowdown costing 3 to 5 points of 2028 growth, which is less than the share price implies. The market also treats the Q4 cash print as a test Asker could pass; we expect the print to look weak against AddLife's for a structural reason, and we would get ahead of that reading.

Score: 50. A simple, monitorable, one-variable case in a non-cyclical business, offset by a binary disclosure event, high leverage, a thin register and two undated, invisible value-chain risks.

#10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Asker is bottoming, not yet turning up; the turn is dated to February to April 2027 and needs two of three conditions.

Evidence for bottoming. The dashboard's rule places the starting phase as Bottoming, and the evidence supports it. Technical momentum is F, with the 200-day average falling in all twelve months and relative strength at the 20th percentile. The 52-week low of SEK 56.2 was set in the weeks after the downgrade and has not been retested. The two-year-forward P/E is 18.7x against a listed range of 16.7 to 34.7x. Revisions are mixed (EBITDA up, EPS and cash down) and the rating mix is two Holds and a Buy. No catalyst arrives before 4 November, and the deciding one arrives in February to April 2027. The dominant broker has moved from Sell to "balanced" without the share price following: SEK 70.8 against targets of SEK 66.5, 82 and 106.

Evidence against a turn having started. Asker has had no quarter of improving cash conversion, no change in disclosure, no positive EPS revision and no technical confirmation.

Inference. If two of the three conditions in the figure arrive, the phase moves to turning up in Q2 2027, and the proof cycle runs to the Q3 2027 report, where Gothenburg savings first show. The thesis broadens only when the acquisition engine visibly re-engages (acquisitions at SEK 200 to 250m a quarter with leverage falling), which on the model's cash flow happens in 2028 to 2029. If the annual report changes nothing, the phase stays at bottoming for another year, and the trough is at risk on any further cash disappointment.

So what. The phase sets the fair multiple (#11): the lower part of the range for a bottoming stock with more uncertain forecasts, not the median. The phase also sets the sizing logic: a bottoming stock with a dated catalyst is a position to build into the catalyst or after it, not one to hold for momentum.

Strongest counter-case. The precedent cohort re-rated eight to nine quarters after its leverage peaks, not four to six months after a critique. If Asker follows the cohort's clock rather than its own calendar, the turn comes in late 2027 or 2028, and the stock is dead money for a year even if the fundamentals are fine. Against that, Asker's leverage peak was lower and its critique came from a broker, both of which argue for a faster clock.

What would change our view. A clean Q4 cash and inventory print in February 2027 would move the phase to turning up before the annual report. A second near-zero statutory cash quarter would move the phase to collapsing (the "false friend" path), regardless of EBITA.

Versus the market. Judging by the share price against the softened broker view, the market's implied phase is somewhere between bottoming and stalling. We agree on bottoming and differ on the clock: we think the company's own calendar sets it, rather than the cohort's precedent.

Score: 40. Bottoming with the turn dated and conditional: below average on current phase, with the next phase visible and four to six months away.

#11The fair multiple

Our fair multiple is 20x two-year-forward P/E on the model's EPS basis (working range 18 to 21x): above the market's 18.7x, below the model's 24x.

The guideline and the data. Viewforth's guideline sets no fair multiple for Asker, because the stock's two-year-forward P/E history is under 24 months long (19 months, from a first observation in May 2025). The dashboard's rule places the phase as Bottoming, and the guideline puts a bottoming or turning stock in the lower part of its range. The range runs from 16.7x to 34.7x on 76 weekly points, with a median of 24.0x, a 25th to 75th percentile band of 21.5x to 28.2x and a 10th to 90th band of 19.6x to 31.2x; the multiple is now 18.7x (9th percentile). The monthly path: 33.0x in May 2025 at SEK 103; 24.1x by December 2025; 19.7x at the February 2026 low (SEK 64); back to 24.2x in May 2026 (SEK 83); and 18.7x in September 2026 (SEK 66.5).

Three cautions before setting a figure.

  1. The history is a de-rating, not a cycle. The nineteen months record a fall from an IPO premium, so the median of 24x is the pre-dispute level, not the midpoint of a range the stock has oscillated around. Regaining 24x within 18 months is the upside case, not the base.
  2. The dashboard's history uses a different EPS basis. The history is on consensus EPS, which sits about 10% below the model's basis (the brokers' 2027 median of SEK 3.29 against the model's SEK 3.53). A given multiple applied to the model's EPS is therefore worth about 10% more in price than the same multiple applied to consensus EPS, so our figure on the model's basis should sit below the equivalent on the brokers' basis.
  3. The cohort gives the cross-checks. AddLife trades at 29.4x trailing P/E (91st percentile) and 17.6x forward EV/EBITA after its re-rating; Vimian at 17x forward EV/EBIT against a 25x average; Lifco at 19 to 21x EV/EBITA after its short report; Storskogen at 10 to 12x; and the Swedish small-cap average at 13.1x 2027 EV/EBITA. Asker trades today at about 15x 2027 adjusted EBITA (EV SEK 31.8bn), against 21 to 22x before September.
Our view: 20xtwo-year-forward P/E on the model's EPS basis, with a working range of 18 to 21x.

The reasoning for 20x. A business compounding adjusted EBITA at 12 to 14%, with 4.5% organic growth, a 10% margin, leverage of 2.0 to 2.2x and contested but improving earnings quality, deserves a modest premium to the Swedish small-cap market. It deserves a discount to the proven self-funded compounders (Lifco and Lagercrantz at 19 to 23x EV/EBITA), and to AddLife until Asker has three years of deleveraging behind it. At SEK 94 a share (20x 2029 EPS of SEK 4.63), the EV is about SEK 43bn including leases and earn-outs: 20x 2027 adjusted EBITA and 17.7x 2028, between AddLife's post-re-rating 17.6x and Asker's own pre-dispute 21x. Our 20x on the model's basis is roughly 22x on the brokers' basis, inside the 25th to 75th percentile band of the stock's history and below its median, which is where a bottoming stock with a dated clearing event belongs. At 17x the stock is priced as if the proof cycle stalls (equivalent to DNB Carnegie's 15x on cash EBITA); at 24x it is priced as if the proof cycle completes in full and Asker re-earns the compounder label.

What moves the fair multiple. Up to 22 to 24x: a FY2026 report that re-presents leverage with earn-outs included and discloses the capitalisation policy, plus leverage printing at or below 2.0x (in 2029 on the model, in 2028 on the Investment Analyst's higher cash flow). Down to 15 to 17x: the severe accounting case, or a disclosed decision to slow acquisitions below SEK 0.8bn a year, which would turn a compounder into a 4.5% organic grower with 2.4x leverage.

Strongest counter-case. The cohort's precedents say that no levered acquirer regained its prior multiple within 24 months of its leverage peak, which argues for 17 to 18x as the base rather than 20x; and the stock's own history is too short to anchor anything. We weight the precedents and still land at 20x, for three reasons: Asker's leverage peak (2.4x) was far below the cohort's (3.5 to 4.4x); its organic growth (4.5 to 5%) is higher than any of theirs was at the trough; and its de-rating was driven by a dispute over definitions rather than by an operating failure.

Versus the market. The model applies about 24x, the market 18.7x, and DNB Carnegie 15x to cash EBITA. We sit at 20x, above the market and below the model, and we describe the model's +52.7% as the return if the proof cycle completes in full, not as the base.

Score: 62. A current multiple at the 9th percentile of its own range and about 15x forward EBITA, against a fair 20x P/E and a cohort that re-rated from similar levels once leverage fell: favourable on the multiple, with the discount justified today and clearable within the horizon.

#12Total shareholder return, Dupont decomposition

At our 20x fair multiple the return is about +31% to December 2027 and +42% over three years; the multiple decides whether the 18-month return is +12% or +53%.

The model's return. At SEK 71.70, the model's 18-month column (to 31 December 2027) gives a total shareholder return (TSR) of +52.7% (42.9% annualised) and a value of SEK 109.49; the three-year column (to 30 June 2029) gives +78.4% (24.0% annualised) and SEK 127.88. The value of SEK 109.49 is about 23.7x the model's 2029 EPS of SEK 4.63, which is the two-year-forward figure at December 2027, so the model is applying the listed-history median to the model's EPS basis. The three-year value is about 24x the earnings two years beyond mid-2029, which the model extrapolates from 2030's SEK 5.14.

The template allocates most of the 18-month return to the multiple because it anchors earnings differently from a simple forward-EPS reading. On the simpler reading, today's price is 18.7x the model's 24-month-forward EPS of SEK 3.83, so the 18-month return decomposes into earnings +21% (SEK 3.83 to 4.63), multiple +26% (18.7x to 23.7x) and dividends +2% (SEK 1.55), compounding to about +53%. On either reading the multiple contributes more than the earnings to the model's return. That profile is the inverse of a compounder's normal profile, and it is exactly the profile of a bottoming stock on a first-quartile multiple.

The Dupont decomposition at 20x. Over 18 months: earnings +21%, multiple +7%, dividends +2% (1.21 x 1.07 + 0.022 = 1.317). Over three years: earnings +30%, multiple +7%, dividends +4%. At 17x the multiple component is -9%, and the return is the earnings growth less the de-rating.

What drives the earnings component, and how secure it is. The +21% to December 2027 is the growth in capitalised EPS from the 2027/2028 blend to 2029: adjusted EBITA rises from about SEK 2,280m (the blend) to SEK 2,701m, the interest share of EBITA falls from 16% to 13%, and the share count stays flat. Two-thirds of the 2027 leg is secured; the 2028 and 2029 legs rest on the acquired engine growing EBITA by 6 to 7% a year from cash flow, which is the undemonstrated part. In the three cash-conversion states, 2029 EPS is about SEK 4.30, 4.63 or 4.95, worth SEK 86, 93 or 99 at 20x before dividends.

±SEK 6the earnings judgement, a share
±SEK 16the multiple judgement (17x to 24x), around 20x

The dividend (a yield of about 1%, rising from SEK 0.70 to 1.00 over the horizon, at 32 to 33% of reported EPS) is immaterial to the case and should stay so, because cash is worth more inside the acquisition engine at 7x than paid out.

What drives the multiple component: company disclosure, almost entirely. The drivers are the FY2026 report's treatment of provisions, capitalisation and the leverage definition; the FY2026 and FY2027 cash prints; and leverage at or below 2.2x. Sector flows barely register (R-squared 11%). The multiple component is therefore both the largest and the most monitorable part of the return.

The downside, expressed the same way. The fair trough of SEK 45 to 50 is a return of -30 to -37%. The shares reach it through the 5% severe accounting case (2027 EPS of about SEK 2.68 at 15x) or through a second near-zero statutory cash quarter that forces a disclosed slowdown. The probability-weighted twelve-month centre is about SEK 75 to 85 (+5 to +19%).

Versus the market. The sell-side targets (SEK 66.5, 82 and 106; mean 89.9) bracket our 18-month fair value of SEK 94, and the model's SEK 109 sits above the highest of them; DNB Carnegie's peer value of SEK 62 equals our 17x case on a cash basis. The market's implied return, at the current multiple with consensus EPS growth, is the earnings-only row less the EPS cuts to come: roughly +15 to +20% over 18 months, which is what a holder receives if the annual report changes nothing.

Score: 65. A +31% 18-month and +42% three-year return at a below-median fair multiple, two-thirds earnings and one-third re-rating, with a +53% full-proof case and a -30 to -37% trough on a 10 to 20% probability: a favourable, well-defined distribution with a fat lower tail.

#13Summary conclusion

The market has priced the bear's reconstruction of Asker's accounts, and our base case is better than that reconstruction; the FY2026 annual report, four to six months away, will decide between them.

What the market has wrong. Asker Healthcare is a capable, defensive, capital-light distributor compounding adjusted EBITA at 12 to 14%, with a margin crossing 10%. Its shares are priced as if the harshest reading of its accounts were true and as if its lenders were about to stop its acquisition engine. Neither is so: cash EBITA is 10 to 15% below adjusted EBITA, not 25%; the covenant leaves more than a turn of headroom; and two-thirds of 2027's EBITA growth is already secured.

What the market has right. The company has presented itself at its most favourable on every line. Its free cash flow conversion has fallen from about 100% to 55 to 65% while inventory days rose for four years, its leverage sits at its self-imposed ceiling, and it has never raised a target or built the reporting apparatus that a listed serial acquirer needs.

What the case turns on. The case turns on one variable (statutory cash conversion), one document (the FY2026 annual report, February to April 2027) and one management choice (to digest acquisitions and prove cash, which the July 2026 language says management has made). The operating outcomes are predictable; the equity outcome is binary for four to six months and then, with about 60% probability, favourable.

The return and the setup. At a fair multiple of 20x the return is +31% over 18 months and +42% over three years, with a full-proof case of +53% and +78% and a fair trough 30 to 37% below the share price. The near-term setup is poor: momentum is F, estimates will be cut, and the Q4 cash print will look weak for structural reasons. The medium-term skew is positive, because the narrative has priced the bear's reconstruction and the base case is better. Asker is a case for the clearing of a cause for concern, in a medium-quality, non-cyclical business on a first-quartile multiple, with the clearing dated and not yet begun.
CThesis's Change Forces' Strength
CFoundations' Robustness
BSetups' Fit/Crispness
CCase Riskiness

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: C. The positive internal forces (Gothenburg, pruning, a motivated new Chair, a shift to digesting acquisitions) are real, dated and modest, and the external forces are neutral with a defensive tilt. The decisive force, a recovery in cash conversion at the enlarged scale, is plausible on the record but undemonstrated.

Foundations' Robustness: C. Non-cyclical demand, distribution-grade moats, top-decile working-capital returns and a strong operator sit alongside a structural margin ceiling of 10 to 12%, a reported ROCE of 8%, leverage at its ceiling and an earnings base 10 to 15% above cash. The foundations are sound in kind and average in strength.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: B. The case cleanly matches the setup "Major CfC Clearing in MQ non-cyclical or better business on Q1 multiple, leading to reversion to normal" (a major clearing of a cause for concern, in a medium-quality non-cyclical or better business on a first-quartile multiple). The cause for concern is nameable (earnings quality and leverage), the clearing event is dated (the FY2026 annual report), the business is non-cyclical and of medium quality, and the multiple is at the 9th percentile. Two things blur the fit: the clearing has not begun, and "normal" rests on a nineteen-month history.

Case Riskiness: C. The case is simple and monitorable: one variable, three dated tests, and 2027 ranges of ±2% for revenue and -6% to +5% for adjusted EBITA. But it carries a binary disclosure event with a fat lower tail, high leverage, a thin register, and two undated value-chain risks (Dutch insurers and founder retention) that would arrive without warning.

End notes

1. Definitions. "Adjusted EBITA" is the company's own measure. EPS is quoted on the model's basis (adjusted EBITA less net financial items, taxed at 24%, over diluted shares) unless another basis is named. The FactSet consensus blends three brokers on three different bases, so it cannot be compared with any single EPS figure except as a growth rate. "Viewforth" and "we" both refer to the authors of this memo. Grades: A 90 to 100, B 75 to 89, C 50 to 74, D 25 to 49, F 1 to 24. Peer and momentum letters in #8 are the dashboard's own readings, not topic grades.

2. The 2025 EPS base. 2025 EPS on the model's basis is SEK 2.38 on FactSet's Viewforth-definition net income (SEK 2.51 on the arithmetic of the Financial Analyst's second set of estimates), so the model's 30% EPS growth for 2026 is partly a base effect.

3. Free cash flow conventions. The two free cash flow figures in #6 differ in tax convention: the model taxes adjusted pre-tax profit, the Investment Analyst's cross-check taxes reported pre-tax profit, and cash tax on share deals sits between the two.

4. Model template. The model's one-page summary displays the guideline fair multiple as 0.00x, which is a display fault; the guideline sets no fair multiple because the history is under 24 months. The template's split of the model's return (+2.2% dividends, +43.3% multiple and +5.1% earnings over 18 months; +3.6%, +35.0% and +29.5% over three years) is shown in the first chart in #12. No model input has been changed: the net-financial-items change in the third and fourth sets of estimates already restored the first set's instruction of "flat to slightly up".

5. Sources and drawing conventions. Default visuals are drawn from model update 2 and the Master Dashboard (made 24 October 2026). History is FactSet's reported basis; consensus is the FactSet median on the brokers' basis; Viewforth figures are from the one-page summary of the Financial Analyst's model. Visuals in visuals/drawn/ and visuals/drawn-copy-editor/ are drawn from the figures in this memo; where a chart shows a range as one bar, the bar is drawn at the middle of the range.
